segments.title: Stakeholders and the cost of poor decisions
segments.script: Decision-making is the action or process of thinking through possible options and selecting one. It is important to recognize that managers are continually making decisions, and that the quality of their decision-making has an impact, sometimes quite significant, on the effectiveness of the organization and its stakeholders. Stakeholders are all the individuals or groups that are affected by an organization (such as customers, employees, shareholders, etc.). Members of the top management team regularly make decisions that affect the future of the organization and all its stakeholders, such as deciding whether to pursue a new technology or product line. A good decision can enable the organization to thrive and survive long-term, while a poor decision can lead a business into bankruptcy. Managers at lower levels of the organization generally have a smaller impact on the organization's survival, but can still have a tremendous impact on their department and its workers. Consider, for example, a first-line supervisor who is charged with scheduling workers and ordering raw materials for her department. Poor decision-making by lower-level managers is unlikely to drive the entire firm out of existence, but it can lead to many adverse outcomes such as: reduced productivity if there are too few workers or insufficient supplies, increased expenses if there are too many workers or too many supplies, particularly if the supplies have a limited shelf life or are costly to store, and frustration among employees, reduced morale, and increased turnover (which can be costly for the organization) if the decisions involve managing and training workers.
keyPoints: Decision-making is the process of thinking through options and selecting one
Stakeholders are all the individuals or groups affected by an organization, such as customers, employees and shareholders
Top managers' decisions can make an organization thrive or drive it into bankruptcy; lower-level managers have a smaller but still real impact
Poor decisions by a first-line manager can lead to reduced productivity, increased expenses, or frustration and turnover among employees
segments.altExplanation: Decisions are not only a top-management concern. A CEO's choice can decide whether the whole company survives, while a supervisor's choice about staffing or supplies decides whether her own department runs smoothly. Both kinds of decisions have real stakeholders who feel the results.
segments.deeper: The chapter returns to this stakeholder idea when it discusses ethics: because decisions affect customers, employees, shareholders and others, managers cannot treat a choice as purely their own. The later sections on decision-making barriers, such as bounded rationality and time pressure, explain why even well-intentioned managers still produce some of these adverse outcomes.

checkpoint.prompt: What are some positive outcomes of decision-making for an organization? What are some possible negative outcomes?
checkpoint.answer: A good decision can help an organization thrive and survive long-term, while a poor decision can drive it into bankruptcy. At lower levels, a poor decision is less likely to threaten the whole firm but can still cause reduced productivity, increased expenses, or frustration, low morale and turnover among employees.
checkpoint.rubric: Must give at least one positive outcome (organization thrives or survives) and at least one negative outcome (bankruptcy, reduced productivity, increased expenses, or employee frustration/turnover), not just a vague 'good or bad things happen'.

checkpoint.prompt: In addition to the owners of a business, who are some of the other stakeholders that managers should consider when making decisions?
checkpoint.answer: Stakeholders also include customers, employees, and shareholders, along with any other individuals or groups affected by the organization's decisions.
checkpoint.rubric: Must name at least two groups besides owners, drawn from customers, employees, or shareholders (or 'other groups affected by the organization').

segments.title: Deciding when to decide
segments.script: While some decisions are simple, a manager's decisions are often complex ones that involve a range of options and uncertain outcomes. When deciding among various options and uncertain outcomes, managers need to gather information, which leads them to another necessary decision: how much information is needed to make a good decision? Managers frequently make decisions without complete information; indeed, one of the hallmarks of an effective leader is the ability to determine when to hold off on a decision and gather more information, and when to make a decision with the information at hand. Waiting too long to make a decision can be as harmful for the organization as reaching a decision too quickly. Failing to react quickly enough can lead to missed opportunities, yet acting too quickly can lead to organizational resources being poorly allocated to projects with no chance of success. Effective managers must decide when they have gathered enough information and must be prepared to change course if additional information becomes available that makes it clear that the original decision was a poor one. For individuals with fragile egos, changing course can be challenging because admitting to a mistake can be harder than forging ahead with a bad plan. Effective managers recognize that given the complexity of many tasks, some failures are inevitable. They also realize that it's better to minimize a bad decision's impact on the organization and its stakeholders by recognizing it quickly and correcting it.
keyPoints: Managers rarely have complete information, so an effective leader must decide when to gather more and when to act
Waiting too long can mean missed opportunities; acting too quickly can waste resources on projects with no chance of success
Effective managers stay ready to change course if new information shows the original decision was poor
Admitting a mistake can feel harder than continuing with a bad plan, especially for people with fragile egos
segments.altExplanation: There are two ways to get the timing of a decision wrong: deciding too soon, before you understand the situation, or deciding too late, after the chance to act has passed. The skill the book describes is judging when you have enough information to move.
segments.deeper: This links to the barriers to decision-making discussed later in the chapter: because managers face real time constraints and incomplete information, waiting for certainty is not an option, and heuristics or shortcuts often fill the gap. The willingness to change course described here is also the opposite of escalation of commitment, where a manager keeps following a decision simply because it has already been made.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does the passage say that waiting too long to decide can be just as harmful as deciding too quickly?
checkpoint.answer: Waiting too long can cause the organization to miss opportunities, while deciding too quickly can lead to resources being poorly allocated to projects that have no real chance of success. Both timing mistakes carry real costs for the organization.
checkpoint.rubric: Must mention both risks: missed opportunities from waiting too long, and resources wasted on doomed projects from deciding too quickly. Naming only one side is partial.

checkpoint.prompt: According to the passage, what makes it hard for some managers to change course after a decision turns out to be poor?
options: They cannot picture every possible alternative
Admitting a mistake feels harder than continuing
They rely on a shortcut instead of new evidence
They want to avoid conflict with their team
checkpoint.answer: Admitting a mistake feels harder than continuing
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option about admitting a mistake being harder than forging ahead with a bad plan, especially for people with fragile egos.

segments.title: Not a multiple-choice test
segments.script: It's also worth noting that making decisions as a manager is not at all like taking a multiple-choice test: with a multiple-choice test there is always one right answer. This is rarely the case with management decisions. Sometimes a manager is choosing between multiple good options, and it's not clear which will be the best. Other times there are multiple bad options, and the task is to minimize harm. Often there are individuals in the organization with competing interests, and the manager must make decisions knowing that someone will be upset no matter what decision is reached. Sometimes managers are asked to make decisions that go beyond just upsetting someone, they may be asked to make decisions in which harm could be caused to others. These decisions have ethical or moral implications. Ethics and morals refer to our beliefs about what is right vs. wrong, good vs. evil, virtuous vs. corrupt. Implicitly, ethics and morals relate to our interactions with and impact on others, if we never had to interact with another creature, we would not have to think about how our behaviors affected other individuals or groups. All managers, however, make decisions that impact others. It is therefore important to be mindful about whether our decisions have a positive or a negative impact. "Maximizing shareholder wealth" is often used as a rationalization for placing the importance of short-term profits over the needs of others who will be affected by a decision, such as employees, customers, or local citizens (who might be affected, for example, by environmental decisions). Maximizing shareholder wealth is often a short-sighted decision, however, because it can harm the organization's financial viability in the future. Bad publicity, customers boycotting the organization, and government fines are all possible long-term outcomes when managers make choices that cause harm in order to maximize shareholder wealth. More importantly, increasing the wealth of shareholders is not an acceptable reason for causing harm to others. As you can see from these brief examples, management is not for the faint of heart! It can, however, be incredibly rewarding to be in a position to make decisions that have a positive impact on an organization and its stakeholders. We see a great example of this in the Sustainability and Responsible Management box.
keyPoints: Unlike a multiple-choice test, management decisions rarely have one clearly right answer
Managers often choose between multiple good options, multiple bad options, or competing stakeholder interests
Some decisions carry ethical or moral implications about right versus wrong and good versus harmful
'Maximizing shareholder wealth' can be a short-sighted rationalization if it causes bad publicity, boycotts, or fines
segments.altExplanation: A test question has a key you can check your answer against; a management decision does not. Sometimes every option available is flawed, or helping one stakeholder means disappointing another, so the manager's job is to weigh outcomes rather than find the single correct one.
segments.deeper: The ethical point here connects back to the stakeholder idea from the start of the section: because decisions affect customers, employees and communities, treating short-term shareholder gain as the only goal ignores the same stakeholders the chapter opened with. This is also the first place the chapter shows a decision that cannot be judged by outcome alone, since a harmful choice can still happen to work out financially in the short run.

checkpoint.prompt: How is managerial decision-making different from a multiple-choice test?
checkpoint.answer: A multiple-choice test always has one right answer, but management decisions rarely do. Managers often choose between multiple good options, multiple bad options, or the competing interests of different people, so someone may be unhappy no matter what is decided.
checkpoint.rubric: Must state that, unlike a test, there is often no single correct answer, and mention multiple good/bad options or competing interests as the reason. A bare 'it's harder' is not enough.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does the passage call 'maximizing shareholder wealth' a short-sighted rationalization?
options: It ignores information that is hard to gather
It keeps managers from changing course later
It can bring bad publicity, boycotts, and fines
It relies on shortcuts instead of full analysis
checkpoint.answer: It can bring bad publicity, boycotts, and fines
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option about long-term harm such as bad publicity, customers boycotting the organization, or government fines.

segments.title: Doing well and doing good
segments.script: The focus of a manager or a business owner is often primarily on doing well (making a profit). Sometimes, though, organizational leaders choose to pursue two big goals at once: doing well, and simultaneously doing good (benefiting society in some way). Why? Generally because they think it's an important thing to do. The business provides an opportunity to pursue another goal that the founders, owners, or managers are also passionate about. In the case of New Belgium Brewing, the company's cofounders, Jeff Lebesch and Kim Jordan, were passionate about two things: making great beer and environmental stewardship. So it should come as no surprise that their brewery is dedicated to reducing its environmental footprint. The brewery has created a culture that fosters sustainability in a wide range of ways, such as by giving employees a bicycle on their one-year anniversary as a way to encourage them to ride bicycles to work. The organization is also active in advocacy efforts, such as the "Save the Colorado" (river) campaign, and it works hard to promote responsible decision-making when it comes to environmental issues. In fact, in 1999, following an employee vote, the brewery began to purchase all of its electricity from wind power, even though it was more expensive than electricity from coal-burning power plants (which meant reduced profitability and less money for employee bonuses).
keyPoints: Some organizational leaders pursue two goals at once: doing well financially and doing good for society
New Belgium Brewing's cofounders were passionate about both making great beer and environmental stewardship
The brewery built a culture of sustainability, including giving employees bicycles and joining river advocacy efforts
In 1999, following an employee vote, the brewery chose to buy wind power even though it was more expensive
segments.altExplanation: New Belgium's founders treated the business as a vehicle for something they also cared about beyond profit. The wind-power decision shows what that commitment costs in practice: the company knowingly accepted lower profitability, and smaller employee bonuses, to act on its environmental values.
segments.deeper: This is the chapter's concrete example of the ethical decision-making idea from the previous section: a decision that trades some short-term profit for a longer-term or broader good. The employee vote before switching to wind power also shows stakeholders, in this case employees, being brought directly into a managerial decision rather than just being affected by it.

checkpoint.prompt: According to the passage, why did New Belgium Brewing switch to purchasing wind power even though it was more expensive?
checkpoint.answer: The brewery's cofounders were passionate about environmental stewardship, and in 1999, after an employee vote, the company chose to buy all of its electricity from wind power even though it cost more and meant reduced profitability and smaller employee bonuses.
checkpoint.rubric: Must mention the founders' commitment to environmental stewardship and that the company accepted a higher cost or lower profitability, ideally noting the employee vote.

checkpoint.prompt: What best describes the two goals New Belgium's cofounders pursued together?
options: Reducing uncertainty in every decision they made
Avoiding conflict and building team consensus
Cutting costs and maximizing shareholder wealth
Making great beer and protecting the environment
checkpoint.answer: Making great beer and protecting the environment
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option naming both making great beer and environmental stewardship or protection.

segments.title: Sustainability pays off
segments.script: While the brewery still relies primarily on wind power, it also now generates a portion of its electricity onsite, some from rooftop solar panels, and even more from biogas, the methane gas byproduct that is created by microbes in the brewery's water treatment plant. The company cleans the wastewater generated from beer production, and in doing so it generates the biogas, which is captured and used for energy to help run the brewery. Brewing is water intensive, so New Belgium works hard to reduce water consumption and to recycle the water that it does use. The company also reduces other types of waste by selling used grain, hops, and yeast to local ranchers for cattle feed. The company, which has been employee owned since 2013, also works with the local utility through a Smart Meter program to reduce their energy consumption at peak times. All of these efforts at doing good must come at a cost, right? Actually, research shows that companies that are committed to sustainability have superior financial performance, on average, relative to those that are not. In coming up with creative ways to reduce, reuse, and recycle, employees often also find ways to save money (like using biogas). In addition, organizations that strive to do good are often considered attractive and desirable places to work (especially by people who have similar values) and are also valued by the surrounding communities. As a result, employees in those organizations tend to be extremely committed to them, with high levels of engagement, motivation, and productivity. Indeed, it seems clear that the employees at the New Belgium Brewery are passionate about where they work and what they do. This passion generates value for the organization and proves that it is, in fact, possible to do well while having also made the decision to do good. And in the case of New Belgium Brewery, that means working to protect the environment while also making delicious beer.
keyPoints: New Belgium now generates some of its own electricity onsite, from rooftop solar and biogas made from treating its wastewater
The company reduces water use and sells leftover grain, hops and yeast to local ranchers for cattle feed
Research shows that companies committed to sustainability tend to have superior financial performance on average
Organizations that do good are often seen as attractive places to work, with more engaged and committed employees
segments.altExplanation: Sustainability here is not framed as charity that costs the business. Treating wastewater produces usable energy, selling waste grain brings in money, and workers who share the company's values tend to stay and perform better, so the environmental and financial goals reinforce each other.
segments.deeper: This closes the New Belgium example by answering the question the chapter poses about ethical decisions: doing good does not have to conflict with doing well. The link between sustainability and financial performance also supports the earlier point that 'maximizing shareholder wealth' at the expense of other stakeholders is often short-sighted, since the passage shows the opposite strategy performing well financially.

checkpoint.prompt: Does the passage say that pursuing sustainability comes at a financial cost to New Belgium Brewing? Explain.
checkpoint.answer: No. The passage says research shows companies committed to sustainability have superior financial performance on average, and that finding creative ways to reduce, reuse and recycle often saves the company money while also attracting committed and engaged employees.
checkpoint.rubric: Must state that sustainability is not shown as costing the business and give a reason, such as better average financial performance, cost savings from reuse, or more engaged and committed employees.

checkpoint.prompt: According to the passage, what byproduct does New Belgium capture from treating its brewery wastewater?
options: Biogas that is used for energy
Grain that is sold to local ranchers
Wind power bought from the utility
checkpoint.answer: Biogas that is used for energy
checkpoint.rubric: Must select biogas as the byproduct captured from treating wastewater and used for energy.
